11056-trial-and-triumph:
Frances E. W. Harper wrote this rediscovered novel about Annette, a mischievous, hard-headed girl who torments her aunt Susan. Annette pours oil on a neighbour's clean steps, upsetting Mrs. Larkins, a proud housekeeper who believes beating is the only cure for bad children. Aunt Susan, mother of six, says all her children together never gave her as much trouble as Annette alone.

Later chapters follow Mr. Thomas, a young man building a business and opening gates to others, generous, conservative in good things, and open to new ideas that make life nobler. Harper links childhood trial to adult triumph, with lessons on discipline, kindness, and self-help. The novel gives readers an African American writer's domestic story, warm, moral, and rooted in community life.
1275-alexandria-and-her-schools-four-lec:
Charles Kingsley, the novelist and clergyman, gives four lectures on Alexandria, the Egyptian city where Greek learning met Jewish and Christian thought. He traces its schools from the Museum and its library through Philo, Clement, and the Neoplatonists, to the city's fall.

Kingsley writes with a Victorian's zeal for the meeting of faith and reason, and his lectures praise Alexandria as a crossroads of minds. The book is short and vivid, if dated in its judgments. It suits readers who like the history of ideas in lecture form. Kingsley's lectures give a vivid, short entry to Alexandria's schools.
2164-the-lumley-autograph:
Susan Fenimore Cooper, identified in Graham's Magazine as the author of Rural Hours, tells a short tale built around an autograph and the Lumley name. Published in 1851, the story turns on letters, reputation, and a scrap of handwriting. Cooper published the tale in Graham's Magazine in 1851, when magazine fiction was booming.

Cooper writes with the care of a daughter of James Fenimore Cooper, and the tale suits readers of mid-century magazine fiction. Its interest lies less in plot than in manners, memory, and the value placed on a famous name. The autograph plot turns on how a signature can carry fame, fraud, or simple human vanity.
22258-tales-of-the-caliph:
Hafiz Adam wrote Tales of the Caliph as new adventures of Haroun Alraschid, the caliph of the Arabian Nights. Haroun was in the habit, as everyone knows, of wandering Baghdad after nightfall in disguise. He went to see that justice was done, Adam admits, but also in hope of adventure. Many of his wanderings are already famous; these, the author promises, are no whit less interesting.

New tales follow the caliph and his vizier through markets, divans, and midnight streets. Justice, wit, and mercy resolve each night's puzzle. The book is an Edwardian imitation of the Arabian Nights, written by an Indian author for English readers. It keeps the old frame with a fresh stock of stories.
26861-the-temple-of-nature-or-the-origin:
Erasmus Darwin, author of The Botanic Garden, Zoonomia, and Phytologia, published this poem with philosophical notes in London in 1803. A preface dated from the Priory near Derby on January 1, 1802, disowns deep reasoning. The poem aims to amuse by bringing nature's operations before the imagination in the order time presented them. Its machinery comes from the Eleusinian mysteries, where a hierophant explained the philosophy of nature to initiates through allegoric scenery.

Canto one treats the production of life, beginning beneath the sea with spontaneous minute animals, irritation, appetency, and sensation. Vegetables and animals improve by reproduction, rocks of shell and coral rise, islands and continents lift by earthquake, and animals emigrate from the sea. The tadpole, the lizard, the beaver, and the whale mark stages of the ascent, and Venus rising from the sea stands as emblem of organic nature.
28221-dorothy-s-triumph:
Evelyn Raymond wrote Dorothy's Triumph, copyright 1911, as a girls' story of music and travel. Dorothy Calvert, humming Maryland, my Maryland on a train, meets Jim Barlow, whose loyalty to New York has softened after a visit to old Bellvieu. Rudolf Mencl drew the pictures, including a melody that sets the heart beating.

Chapters follow Dorothy to a mountain camp, a cry in the night, unwelcome visitors, and lessons with Herr Deichenberg, whose concert crowns her work. A Christmas at Bellvieu, an offer from Mr. Ludlow, and a storm test her. The novel ends, as its title promises, in triumph.
31779-from-bondage-to-liberty-in-religio:
George T. Ashley's 1919 spiritual autobiography, published by the Beacon Press at Boston, traces his passage from bondage to liberty in religion. Its eight chapters run from childhood, youth, and education through seeking liberty, new visions and disturbances, nearer the crisis, the crisis itself, and a new confession of faith.

Ashley opens by noting that practically all people inherit their first religious opinions from parents and early environment, and most never get beyond that stage. Readers get a liberal religious memoir, frank about inherited creeds, doubt, and the search for a faith examined rather than merely received.
34362-joseph-smith-as-scientist-a-contri:
John Widtsoe wrote this contribution to Mormon philosophy, published at Salt Lake City in 1908 by the General Board of the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Associations. Widtsoe opens by granting that Joseph Smith's mission was spiritual, so scientific discussion is not to be expected in the Prophet's writings. Yet the Church, he says, counts all human knowledge and the laws of nature as part of its religious system.

Twenty-one chapters then set Mormon teaching beside modern science. Early chapters treat the indestructibility of matter and of energy, the universal ether, and the reign of law. Later ones take up the new astronomy, geological time, organized intelligence, and the law of evolution. Faith, repentance, baptism, and the Word of Wisdom are handled as laws governing the individual, and an appendix offers the testimony of the soil.
34765-the-story-of-the-atlantic-telegrap:
Henry M Field wrote a history of the Atlantic telegraph, its title page listing his travel books from Killarney to Egypt and Japan. Field was brother to Cyrus Field, the cable's chief promoter. The book tells how a telegraph line was laid under the Atlantic Ocean. Early attempts, failures, and the final success of 1866 structure the story.

Contemporary accounts treated the cable as the wonder of the age. Field wrote as a participant's brother with access to the principals. His narrative preserves speeches, voyages, and the 1858 collapse. Later editions kept the story current as cables multiplied. The work remains a first hand source for the enterprise that first wired the ocean.
36830-the-badger-a-monograph:
The Badger, a monograph by Alfred Pease, was issued at London in 1898. Pease had written on the Cleveland hounds and on horse breeding for farmers. A front plate shows the badger in its sett country. A motto on hunting as the noblest exercise heads the work.

A monograph gives one animal the full treatment of a book. Pease treats the habits, haunts, and hunting of the badger in turn. The badger was dug and baited in that age, and also studied. Country readers took such books as guides to a shy night beast. Pease writes as a sportsman with a naturalist’s patience. His badger is neither pet nor vermin, but a strong old tenant of the woods. The book holds a full portrait of the animal and its lore.
37537-san-francisco-in-ruins-a-pictorial:
Givens took eight score photos of San Francisco in its worst days. The book came out in 1906, the year of the great quake. Its theme is quake harm, fire's waste, and relief camps. A first plate names the chief staff who held the town. Funston, who led the troops of that coast, heads that list.

Street by street, the plates show walls down and ash in heaps. Camps of tents house the lost in row on row of white. Ships, troops, and bread lines show the aid at work. Few words stand with the plates, for the views speak loud. Past fans get a town's dire days in true light. The book was made while ash was still warm.
37888-charlotte-bronte-a-monograph:
Charlotte Bronte, a Monograph, is a life of the novelist by T Wemyss Reid, issued at London in eighteen seventy seven. The hosted copy is the third edition. A portrait of her father, the Reverend Patrick Bronte, stands at its front. The book is inscribed to Lord Houghton. It calls itself a memorial of a life that added new glory to the literary history of Yorkshire.

In his preface Reid says the life and genius of Charlotte Bronte had long engaged his attention. He wrote at the request of a lady who supplied most of his original materials, he says. He owns his own deficiencies in the task. He trod in the footsteps of Mrs Gaskell, he notes, and held back from writing much on that account. Friends known and unknown sustained him, he adds.
4347-my-young-alcides-a-faded-photograph:
Charlotte M. Yonge called this novel a faded photograph, and its subtitle points to its game: a modern Hercules in a shooting-coat. In her preface she admits the idea insisted on being worked out, even at the risk of travestying the Farnese statue in country dress. The Greek myth, she notes, also echoes Samson of old.

The chapters translate the labors into English life: the Arghouse inheritance, the lion of Neme Heath, the dragon's head, the capture in the snow, and the champion's belt. A strong young hero faces cattle stealers, a bloodhound, and golden fruit. Yonge turns myth into a domestic adventure, with morals as well as marvels.
46707-the-nurserymatograph:
The Nurserymatograph is a jest book on the new art of film shows. Its front page credits the text to a law man, the mid bits to a church man, and the drawn plates to a war man. It came out at London in the year past the great war but two. Fake ads for gear, mats, and lamps crowd its first pages.

A mock list of past works by its hand claims sets of seven and of past ten books on the film craft, one set dated in a year yet to come. The text then walks past how a film is made, from the crowd of guests to the names of the stars. Palaces of film are mocked as dim barns or false grand halls. The tone is dry fun at the craze of the new shows.
5075-the-lion-of-the-north-a-tale-of-the:
G. A. Henty's Lion of the North opens late on a spring afternoon in 1630. Clouds mass over the hilltops of southern Scotland. Fierce wind drives rain before it. Three days of rain have turned every mountain burn into a boiling torrent. Rivers have flooded the low valleys. Evening closes in as a lad of sixteen gazes across the swollen Nith rushing past in turbid flood.

The invitation of the first chapter draws the boy toward Gustavus Adolphus and the Thirty Years' War, where a Scottish lad finds his fortune among Swedish armies. Henty's tale mixes history with adventure in his usual brisk style. Readers get a story of the Lion of the North's wars, seen through young Scottish eyes.
50864-a-story-of-the-telegraph:
John Murray made A Story of the Telegraph at Montreal, printed by Lovell and Son in 1905. Murray calls the book a small compendium of telegraph history for the lay public. Its facts come from the chief standard works on the theme. Short lives of famed men of science and of inventors let readers judge each claim for themselves. Murray held out hope of a larger book to come.

The part on first telegraph men in Canada gets the warmest stress. Murray says it should hold Canadians most, with tales from the early wires. Some names of worth had to be left out to keep the book small. An opening survey calls the electric telegraph one of the most prized tools of public life. The book shows how a wire shrank weeks of wait to minutes.
53785-the-violin-and-old-violin-makers-b:
The Violin and Old Violin Makers is a historical and biographical account of the violin by Mason Clarke, author of a Biographical Dictionary of Fiddlers. William Reeves of London, a publisher of books on music, issued it. The title promises facsimiles of the labels of the old makers. Its frontispiece shows a copy of the Gasparo da Salo violin used by Ole Bull, the famous Scandinavian violinist.

Clarke's preface explains the book's odd birth. Years earlier he had finished a large, exhaustive work on the violin. Its first portion reached the stereotype stage, but a fire destroyed the plates. Other business pressed, and the work was laid aside. Since then other violin books had appeared, which might seem to make another superfluous. Musical friends urged him instead to produce a popular work at a low price.
60599-women-of-belgium-turning-tragedy-t:
Charlotte Kellogg wrote Women of Belgium, in a sixth edition dated nineteen seventeen, with a foreword by Herbert C Hoover. Hoover chaired the Commission for Relief in Belgium. Kellogg's subtitle promises tragedy turned to triumph.

Belgium, she writes, had been the cockpit of Europe for centuries of pain. A hundred years of peace then made it the beehive of the continent. Eight million folk lived on a small area, rich by thrift and industry. Chapters treat the soup kitchens, cradles on the Meuse, and a group called the Little Bees. Lace work, toy factories, and care for maimed men follow. A front picture shows a dining room for frail children.
6444-the-boys-of-bellwood-school-or-fran:
Frank V. Webster follows Frank Jordan of Tipton in The Boys of Bellwood School, subtitled Frank Jordan's Triumph. A stickpin opens the trouble. Frank bought it at Mace's jewelry store with money he earned, but his aunt calls him extravagant. She says circumstances do not alter cases when a boy is a spendthrift. Frank lives with miserly, fault finding Miss Tabitha Brown while his invalid father seeks health in the South, his mother nursing him there.

For nearly a month the lad has not enjoyed life very greatly, and two thoughts fill his mind most. Later chapters promise a tinker boy, a diamond bracelet, Gill Mace, a ruined house, an astonishing clue, and a confidence man. A mid scene shows a farmer running a swindler down a railway car and tossing him toward a ditch by the depot. Webster writes schoolboy adventure with a hero earning his own way.
64488-roman-stoicism-being-lectures-on-t:
E Vernon Arnold wrote Roman Stoicism, lectures on the history of the Stoic philosophy with special reference to its development within the Roman Empire, issued at Cambridge in 1911. Arnold was professor of Latin at the University College of North Wales. He had been a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. The book is given in Latin to his teacher Henrico Jackson.

A list of fixes treats Greek accents and note references at the front. Quotes in the notes are keyed to von Arnim's Stoic fragments, Arnold says. Corrections span pages one hundred and five to four hundred and twenty three. The lectures trace Stoic thought from its Greek roots to its Roman form. Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius stand in that Roman line, as the theme implies. The book suits students of classics and philosophy who want a clear history.
71118-brownie-s-triumph:
Georgie Sheldon wrote Brownie's Triumph, a novel whose copyrights run from 1879 to 1901 under Street and Smith, reissued in New York by the Burt Company. Sheldon wrote many popular romances, among them Virgie's Inheritance and His Heart's Queen. The story opens at three o'clock on September 5, 1876, in Memorial Hall at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia.

Brownie Douglas, bright and small, is called back by her friend Aspasia. The two young ladies make a study in contrast. Aspasia is tall, fair, languid, and dressed in the height of fashion, with jewels, laces, and a long train that demands all her attention. Brownie looks sixteen, though she is eighteen, and takes the wonders around her with eager eyes. Sheldon builds her tale on that contrast of wealth, show, and quick life.
71304-a-mechanical-and-critical-enquiry-:
James Parsons, a doctor and Fellow of the Royal Society, printed his study of hermaphrodites in London in seventeen forty-one. He called it a mechanical and critical enquiry, and he gave the book to Sir Hans Sloane and the Royal Society. Parsons set out to clear away old error on a hard subject.

He argues against the view that true mixed sex occurs in human bodies. He then gives a past account of how such births were explained and what laws said about them. A long chapter weighs what other writers had claimed. The book ends with notes on a foetus and on cuts made by other hands.
72721-beryl-s-triumph:
Beryl Triumph is a girls story by Eglanton Thorne, from the Religious Tract Society. The book was formerly issued as Coral and Beryl before this printing. Coloured illustrations dress the London tract society edition for young buyers. Contents open with Beryl, then The Shipwreck and A Friendless Sufferer in the tale.

Beryl makes a request, has perplexing thoughts, and hears talk about the kingdom. A strange Sunday school, children missing, and deliverance from the tide fill the middle. The governess, falling into temptation, and self will and sorrow test the heroine. A frontispiece shows Beryl striking out bravely through the water for someone.
7356-the-boy-scout-camera-club-or-the-co:
Scout Master G. Harvey Ralphson's Boy Scout Camera Club, or The Confession of a Photograph, opens with Frank crying that a child's face looks down from above. Its chapters promise a lost foreign prince, a hole in the attic floor, a box's contents, a camp in the mountain, and signals in the canyon. A mint in the mountains, Uncle Ike, a lank mule as decoy, and Jack's elegant chicken pie follow. The black hand game, three days to move in, and a night on the summit complete the list.

The scouts' camera turns detective, as a photograph confesses what eyes missed. Ralphson writes brisk boys' adventure, mixing camp craft with mystery and humour. Young readers get scouting, sleuthing, and mountain fun in one lively tale.
74682-the-life-of-the-emperor-francis-jo:
The Life of the Emperor Francis Joseph is a biography by Francis Gribble, printed in London by Eveleigh Nash in 1914. A photograph by Bieber shows the old emperor. Gribble opens with a paradox: two emperors, William of Germany and Francis Joseph of Austria, might seem well covered by earlier books. The ground, he argues, is not covered at all.

No life of Francis Joseph, and no history of Austria, joins the personal and the political in their true relation. Earlier writers assumed that tittle-tattle is tittle-tattle and history is history, and that the two can never meet. The two things, Gribble answers, are liable to meet anywhere. Personality, of a man and of a house, can be gauged only by studying both. His life of the aged emperor appeared in the very year the emperor's world went to war.
749-barlaam-and-ioasaph:
A tale long ascribed to St. John of Damascus tells of Ioasaph, a prince shut away from sorrow, and Barlaam, the hermit who teaches him the Christian faith. The text was likely translated into Greek in the eleventh century from an older eastern source. It follows the prince as he meets age, sickness, and death for the first time and seeks the truth behind them.

Parables and debates carry the teaching, with stories inside the story that linger in the mind. The work blends Indian legend with Christian thought, and it travelled across Europe for centuries. It matters as a bridge between East and West, and as one of the most loved religious romances of the Middle Ages.
75683-the-telephone-the-microphone-the-p:
Count Du Moncel wrote a book on the telephone, the microphone, and the phonograph, shown here in a fourth edition at London in 1892. The English text was passed by the author, who added and fixed parts. Seventy wood cuts show the tools. Du Moncel was a member of the Institut in France.

First parts trace the past of the telephone and show song tools by Reiss and Gray. Bell's phone and its base rules get long space. Battery phones by Edison and more fill the next parts. New forms with more than one plate close the phone part. Later parts treat the microphone and the phonograph in like depth.
79169-esther-s-triumph:
Emma Leslie wrote Esther's Triumph, for the Religious Tract Society at London. Leslie had written Maggie's Message and Dearer than Life before it. A plate shows Rhoda taken in motherly arms by a friend. Contents open with Esther's home, then Rhoda Morris herself. A mysterious disappearance and brother and sister follow in the list.

At the circus, alone in the world, and in the workhouse come next. Chapter one opens on a point of speech and conscience. Esther Wright scolds her friend for praising Rhoda's loose talk. To say goodness gracious is vulgar, Esther holds, and near to vain swearing. Rhoda is poorly dressed, in a washed-out plaid frock, the tale notes. At examinations Rhoda was always first ready with an answer, it owns. Leslie gives a schoolgirl's pride and fall in tract dress.
8443-the-mysteries-of-montreal-being-rec:
Charlotte Fuhrer, a physician with over thirty years of practice in Montreal, writes of things she has seen in that city. Told with the skill of a Dumas or a Collins, they might astonish and startle readers. Her Mysteries of Montreal gathers recollections of a female physician, cases and scenes from a long career, under the motto that truth is stranger than fiction.

The book belongs to the city-mysteries genre, but with a doctor's authority behind it: hospitals, homes, and streets seen from inside medicine. Readers get Victorian Montreal through a woman professional's eyes, a rare viewpoint for its time. The cases, told as stories, mix sensation with social observation.
979-heroes-of-the-telegraph:
J. Munro wrote these lives of the heroes of the telegraph, men who wired the world. Munro, author of Electricity and Its Uses and Pioneers of Electricity, tells how Morse, Wheatstone, and their peers turned sparks into messages, and how cables crossed seas and continents.

Munro writes with a popular, admiring tone, mixing biography with clear accounts of circuits, keys, and codes. His heroes are workers as much as geniuses, and their triumphs came through trial and error. The book is a vivid record of the Victorian communications revolution, for readers who like science told through lives.
alexandria-and-her-schools-four-lectures:
Charles Kingsley delivered these four lectures at the Philosophical Institution in Edinburgh, and the text here follows the 1902 Macmillan printing of his historical lectures. His subject is Alexandria in Egypt, the great seat of learning in the ancient world. Kingsley admits in his preface that the subject was chosen for him and that the lectures are rough.

He traces the city's museum and library, its Greek philosophers, its Jewish scholars, and its early Christian teachers, who tried to wed faith to Greek thought. Figures such as Philo, Origen, and Hypatia pass through the account. The lectures show a Victorian clergyman reading ancient learning with warmth and strong opinions.
barlaam-and-ioasaph:
Barlaam and Ioasaph retells, in Christian dress, the legend of a prince who renounces his throne for the religious life. The hermit Barlaam secretly instructs the Indian prince Ioasaph, sheltered by his father from all knowledge of suffering, and converts him through parables. The 1914 Harvard edition, translated by G R Woodward and H Mattingly, supplies this text.

Tradition ascribes the work to Saint John of Damascus, though scholars believe the Greek version came from a Georgian original around the eleventh century. Behind it stands the life of the Buddha, carried west and baptized. Ioasaph's debates on God, righteousness, and the making of all things fill the middle chapters. Few medieval tales traveled farther.
britannica-1911-abercromby-sir-ralph:
Sir Ralph Abercromby receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. Abercromby, a British lieutenant-general born in 1734, set aside the Scots bar for a cornet's place in 1756. Frederick's methods, seen in the Seven Years' War, formed his tactical mind.

Sympathy with the American colonists kept him near idle till 1793. Holland service, a wound, and a hard retreat won him the Bath in 1795. West Indies command took Grenada, Demerara, St Lucia, and Trinidad. Ireland in 1797 saw him guard civil rule against army abuse, and resign when thwarted. Holland in 1799 proved his gifts again despite disaster. Egypt against the French was set as his next command when the entry's account breaks toward 1801.
britannica-1911-ackermann-rudolph:
Rudolph Ackermann (1764-1834) was an Anglo-German inventor and publisher. He was born at Schneeberg in Saxony. He worked as a saddler and coach-builder for ten years. His work took him to German cities, Paris, and London. In 1795 he opened a print shop in the Strand. He added a drawing school to it. There he set up a lithographic press. He used it to illustrate his monthly Repository of Arts. That journal ran to forty volumes.

Enterprise marks the whole career. Ackermann patented a waterproofing method in 1801. It worked for both paper and cloth. He built a Chelsea factory for it. He pioneered gas lighting in his own premises. In 1825 he launched the popular English Annuals. Forget-me-not was the first of them. His books include the Microcosm of London.
britannica-1911-addison-joseph:
Joseph Addison, an English writer of essays and verse born in sixteen seventy two, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Lancelot Addison, later dean of Lichfield. Born at his father rectory at Milston in Wiltshire, he passed through more than one school. The last was the Charterhouse in London.

He went to Oxford at about age fifteen. He first joined one college, then won a post at a second on the strength of his Latin verse. He took his higher degree in sixteen ninety three and held a post there till seventeen eleven. His first works in print were poems, most of them in Latin in the style of the day. A set of such verse kept his early work safe for readers. The entry then leads on to the prose fame that made his name last.
britannica-1911-adelung-johann-christoph:
Johann Christoph Adelung is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Adelung was a German grammarian and student of language, born in Pomerania in 1732. He was schooled at Anklam and Klosterbergen and studied at the university of Halle. In 1759 he became a professor at the gymnasium of Erfurt.

He gave up that post after two years and settled at Leipzig. There he gave himself wholly to the study of language. In 1787 he became chief librarian to the elector of Saxony at Dresden. He stayed in Dresden until his death in 1806. The entry stresses the vast size of his written output. Every work, it says, shows his genius, industry, and learning. His excellent grammars and his dictionary are named first among his gifts to German letters.
britannica-1911-albo-joseph:
Joseph Albo, a Spanish Jewish thinker of the fifteenth century, asked a sharp question: how few beliefs can hold up a whole faith? His much-read book on the philosophy of Judaism, Iqqarim, or Fundamentals, took up that classic problem for Jewish thought. Which teachings are truly basic, and which ones rest on those?

Maimonides, back in the twelfth century, had counted thirteen principles. Albo cut the list to three: God exists, revelation is real, and God rewards and punishes human deeds. He also led the way in playing down Messianism when setting out Jewish belief. Yet he stood firm on Moses as author of the Law and on tradition as binding. His gift was in telling the vital from the less vital, in practice and in belief alike. An English version came out in the Hebrew Review.
britannica-1911-aqiba-ben-joseph:
ʿAqība ben Joseph (c. 50–132) was a Jewish Palestinian rabbi. He belonged to the circle called tana. Traditions about his life mix truth and legend. Separating them is almost impossible, the entry warns. He became chief teacher at Jaffa's rabbinical school. Tradition credits him with 24,000 scholars. Rabbi Meir was certainly among his pupils. Through Meir, his influence shaped the Mishnah deeply.

Politics brought his violent end. He sided with Bar Cochebas against Rome. He recognised Bar Cochebas as the Messiah. He even acted as his sword-bearer. Roman forces captured him under Julius Severus. They flayed him alive with great cruelty. Tradition praises his steadfastness and composure. He ranks among the ten Jewish martyrs. Synagogue penitential prayer still names them. He first systematised the Jewish tradition. His school produced Aquila's Greek scripture translation.
britannica-1911-arch-joseph:
Joseph Arch, born in 1826, was an English politician who founded the National Agricultural Labourers' Union. His home was Barford, a village in Warwickshire. His parents were of the labouring class. From his mother he took a strong sense of self-worth. He hated the bowing and scraping that the catechism asked of men toward their so-called betters. He taught himself by hard, steady work.

In 1872 Arch set up his union and served as its president. Farm wages rose at that time. That gain broke the union, in a strange turn. The men felt their aim was won and stopped their campaign. Arch kept his good name all the same. In 1885 north-west Norfolk sent him to parliament. His stand for Irish Home Rule cost him the seat in 1886. The Commons held him in respect. Few men of his kind, the piece says, were so free of cheap crowd-play.
britannica-1911-autran-joseph:
The sea made Joseph Autran's name. La Mer of 1835, reworked in 1852 as Les Poèmes de la mer, is his best-known work, and Ludibria ventis followed in 1838. Their success won him the post of librarian in his home town. Vie rurale, in 1856, pictured peasant life; Algerian campaigns fed his soldier verses, among them Milianah, honouring a heroic town defence in 1842, and Laboureurs et soldats. His tragedy La Fille d'Eschyle won at the Odéon, and the French Academy took him in during 1868.

Autran (1813–1877) was a French poet born at Marseilles in June 1813. In 1832 he sent an ode to Lamartine, then at Marseilles on his way east. The older poet talked Autran's father into letting the young man follow his bent for verse, and Autran stayed Lamartine's faithful disciple from then on. He died at Marseilles in 1877.
britannica-1911-bajza-joseph:
Bajza, Joseph (1804-1858), was a Hungarian poet and critic. He was born at Szücsi in 1804. His first writings went to Kisfaludy's Aurora. He edited that literary paper from 1830. He kept the post until 1837. Other journals took much of his work.

His dramatic criticism won the highest praise. In 1830 he published translated foreign plays. His own poems came out in 1835. In 1837 he directed Pest's new national theatre. History then claimed several years. His Historical Library ran to six volumes. A Modern Plutarch and a Universal History followed. Much of that work translated German authors. In 1848 Kossuth made him editor. The paper was Kossuth's own journal. Brain disease struck Bajza in 1850. He died eight years later.
britannica-1911-barnby-sir-joseph:
Sir Joseph Barnby (1838–1896) was an English composer and conductor, son of an organist, born at York on 12 August 1838. A chorister at York Minster from the age of seven, he studied at the Royal Academy of Music. In 1862 he became organist of St Andrew's, Wells Street, in London. There he raised the services to a high standard.

Barnby conducted his own choir from 1864 and, succeeding Gounod in 1871, the Albert Hall Choral Society until his death. He was director of music at Eton from 1875 and principal of the Guildhall School of Music from 1892, the year of his knighthood. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his oratorio Rebekah, his anthems, and his 246 hymn tunes, among them the popular part-song Sweet and Low.
britannica-1911-barthez-paul-joseph:
Paul Joseph Barthez (1734–1806), a French physician born at Montpellier, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He took his doctor's degree at Montpellier in 1753. Army service in Normandy and Westphalia followed, until hospital fever shaped his early career, and he later edited journals in Paris. A medical professorship at Montpellier followed in 1759, and in 1774 he became joint chancellor of the university there.

Barthez is remembered for one idea above all. In Nouveaux élémens de la science de l'homme (1778) he used the term “vital principle” for the unknown cause of life. He did not bind that cause to a spiritual or a material nature. Later works treated the mechanics of movement in men and animals and the treatment of gout. The Revolution cost him much of his fortune and drove him into retirement at Carcassonne.
britannica-1911-bell-george-joseph:
George Joseph Bell (1770–1843) was a Scottish jurist born at Edinburgh, elder brother of Sir Charles Bell. He skipped a full university course but heard lectures by Tytler, Dugald Stewart and Hume. He joined the Faculty of Advocates in 1791 and became a close friend of Francis Jeffrey.

Bell’s Treatise on the Law of Bankruptcy in Scotland grew into his Commentaries on the Law of Scotland, a work praised by jurists such as Story and Kent. He took the Edinburgh chair of Scots law in 1821 and headed the 1833 inquiry into bankruptcy law, whose reports reshaped the rules. His shorter Principles became a standard student text.
britannica-1911-bellamy-joseph:
Joseph Bellamy (1719–1790) was an American theologian born in Cheshire, Connecticut. He graduated from Yale in 1735, studied under Jonathan Edwards, and was licensed to preach while still in his teens. From 1740 until his death he served one parish, the Congregational church at Bethlehem, Connecticut.

True Religion Delineated, printed in 1750, made Bellamy’s name on both sides of the Atlantic. Though he rarely left his parish, his thought shaped his age in America, second only to Edwards in reach. He trained young clergy in classes at his home for years, sending preachers across New England. His Works came out in three volumes after his death.
britannica-1911-berkeley-miles-joseph:
Miles Joseph Berkeley (1803–1889) was an English botanist born at Biggin Hall in Northamptonshire. Rugby and Christ’s College, Cambridge, educated him, and he took holy orders, serving as incumbent of Apethorpe from 1837 and vicar of Sibbertoft from 1868. The country parson’s life left room for a second career in science.

Berkeley won early love for cryptogamic botany, the study of flowerless plants, and became Britain’s leading authority on fungi and plant disease. Some six thousand fungus species are credited to his naming. His Introduction to Cryptogamic Botany of 1857 shows the breadth of his grasp. So do his Gardener’s Chronicle papers on vegetable pathology. His investigations of the potato murrain are singled out for praise.
britannica-1911-bingham-joseph:
Joseph Bingham (1668–1723) was an English scholar and divine, born at Wakefield in Yorkshire. He was educated at University College, Oxford, and became a fellow in 1689. A sermon of his on the terms Person and Substance in the Fathers drew a charge of heresy. The entry calls that charge most unjust. Still, he had to give up his fellowship and leave Oxford. Dr John Radcliffe gave him the rectory of Headbournworthy in 1695.

In that country quiet he began his great work, Origines Ecclesiasticae. Its ten volumes on the antiquities of the Christian church appeared from 1708 to 1722. The design was to set early church customs under clear heads, like works on Greek and Roman antiquities. The 1911 Britannica entry praises the learning and fairness of the result. Bingham lost nearly all his small property in the South Sea Bubble of 1720. He died in August 1723.
britannica-1911-black-joseph:
Joseph Black (1728–1799) was a Scottish chemist and physicist born at Bordeaux, where his father worked in the wine trade. He was schooled in Belfast and studied medicine at Glasgow under William Cullen. His study of lime-water and mild alkalis led him to the work that made his name.

Black showed that heating magnesia alba drove off a gas he called fixed air, and that the lost weight came back when the gas was taken up again. In plain terms, he proved that caustic action meant losing something, not gaining fire-stuff as older theory held. The entry also covers his later career, his few published papers, and the lectures printed after his death in 1803.
britannica-1911-boulay-de-la-meurthe-ant:
Antoine Jacques Claude Joseph Boulay de la Meurthe (1761–1840) was a French lawyer who helped write Napoleon's constitution and civil code. Born at Chamousey in the Vosges, a farm labourer's son, he was called to the bar at Nancy in 1783 and soon made a name in Paris as a speaker. He backed the revolutionary cause in Lorraine and fought at Valmy and Wissembourg.

His moderate views forced him into hiding during the Terror. He sat for La Meurthe in the Council of Five Hundred and twice presided over it, drifting steadily conservative. Fearing a new Terror, he joined the plot that overthrew the Directory in November 1799. Napoleon set him to head the commission drafting the new constitution, and he examined and revised the draft civil code. Eight years settling land titles taken at the Revolution close the account.
britannica-1911-butler-joseph:
Joseph Butler (1692-1752) was an English churchman and philosopher who became bishop of Durham, and his early life fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Wantage, the son of a Presbyterian linen-draper, he was meant for the ministry of that church. He studied at a dissenting academy at Gloucester and then at Tewkesbury.

The entry tells how he grew doubtful of Presbyterian teaching and chose to join the Church of England. At the same time he studied Samuel Clarke's work on the being of God, and at twenty-two wrote to Clarke in secret with sharp questions. Clarke's grave, careful reply showed his high regard for the young man's mind.
britannica-1911-caldecott-randolph:
Randolph Caldecott (1846–1886) was an English artist and illustrator. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his short career. He was born at Chester on 22 March 1846. From 1861 to 1872 he worked as a bank clerk. He clerked first at Whitchurch, then at Manchester. All his spare time went to drawing. In 1872 he moved to London and studied at the Slade School.

Caldecott soon won a wide name as an illustrator. His manner was genial and humorous. He also painted and sculpted, with less success. His chief books illustrated Washington Irving's works. Old Christmas appeared in 1876, and Bracebridge Hall in 1877. From 1878 he made picture-books for children. John Gilpin and The House that Jack Built were among them. His health broke down in 1876. After long suffering he died in Florida on 12 February 1886.
britannica-1911-caliph:
Caliph is a title borne by the heads of the Muslim state. The word in Arabic means successor or representative. This 1911 Britannica article traces the office through history. Abu Bekr first bore the title. On Mahomet's death he became civil and religious head of the state. The Koran also uses the word of Adam and David.

Abu Bekr and his next successors are called the “perfect” caliphs. Thirteen Omayyad caliphs then ruled from Damascus. Thirty-seven Abbasid caliphs followed them at Bagdad. Their line fell before the Turks in 1258. Titular Abbasid caliphs then lived on in Egypt until 1517. Rival lines claimed the title elsewhere too. The Spanish Omayyads held it at Cordova from 755 to 1031. The Fatimite rulers of Egypt claimed it as well. The article closes on the rival tests of legitimacy. Shi'ites demand descent from the Prophet himself. Sunnites require membership of his own tribe.
britannica-1911-caryl-joseph:
Joseph Caryl (1602–1673) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English Nonconformist divine born in London. He graduated at Exeter College, Oxford, and became preacher at Lincoln's Inn. He preached often before the Long Parliament and sat in the Westminster Assembly of 1643. By order of parliament he attended Charles I at Holmby House, and in 1650 he went with John Owen to accompany Cromwell to Scotland.

In 1662 Caryl was ejected from his church of St Magnus near London Bridge. He went on ministering to an Independent congregation in London until his death in March 1673, when John Owen succeeded him. His piety and learning show in his huge commentary on Job, which ran to twelve quarto volumes between 1651 and 1666. A second edition followed in two folio volumes in 1676 and 1677. The entry presents a scholar preacher whose great work outlasted his pulpit.
britannica-1911-cenotaph: Cenotaph is a very short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, two sentences long. The word joins two Greek words, one meaning empty and one meaning tomb. A cenotaph is a monument or tablet raised to the memory of a person whose body lies buried elsewhere. The entry adds the custom's origin. It arose from monuments built for those whose bodies could not be recovered, as in cases of drowning.
britannica-1911-chalier-joseph:
Joseph Chalier, who lived from 1747 to 1793, was a French revolutionary leader. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his rise and fall at Lyons. His family meant him for the church, but he went into trade. He traveled widely for a Lyons firm before 1789.

In Paris Chalier met Marat and Robespierre and took up their cause. Back in Lyons he led town work and taxed the rich to spare the poor. He later led the Jacobin clubs and urged arrests of royalist foes. Town sections rose against his party in May 1793. He was seized, tried, and put to death by the guillotine in July. His followers honored him as a martyr for liberty.
britannica-1911-champollion-figeac-jacqu:
Jacques Joseph Champollion-Figeac, a French archaeologist who lived from 1778 to 1867, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the elder brother of Jean Francois Champollion, the famed reader of Egyptian hieroglyphs. He was born at Figeac in the department of Lot. He became professor of Greek and librarian at Grenoble.

His part in the Hundred Days forced him to retire from Grenoble in 1816. He afterwards became keeper of manuscripts at the national library in Paris. He also took a chair of palaeography, the study of old handwriting and documents. The entry places his life beside the long list of works by his younger brother, which opens the hosted text. Those works include an Egyptian grammar and dictionary edited by Jacques Joseph after his brother's early death.
britannica-1911-cowen-joseph:
Joseph Cowen (1831–1900) was an English politician and journalist, son of Sir Joseph Cowen of Newcastle upon Tyne. His father was a marked citizen and mine-owner of that town. The son was schooled at Edinburgh University. In 1874 he was elected to parliament for the borough on his father's death. His father had held that seat as a Liberal since 1865.

The son stood as a strong Radical on home questions at that time. He backed co-operation and praised Garibaldi, Mazzini and Kossuth. Irish Nationalism won his sympathy as well. In speech, dress and manner he made himself one with the North-country mining class. Short and uncouth in looks, he first shocked the Commons. Earnest force then won the House over to respect. Free of party ties and rough in speech, he rose fast to fame. He was an Imperialist when Liberalism at large shunned that creed.
britannica-1911-cudworth-ralph:
Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) was an English philosopher born at Aller in Somersetshire, son of the rector there. His stepfather, Dr Stoughton, schooled him at home, and he went to his father's college, Emmanuel, at Cambridge. He became a fellow in 1639 and a noted tutor. In 1645 he was made master of Clare Hall and Regius professor of Hebrew. He stood as a leader of the group called the Cambridge Platonists.

Cudworth preached religious toleration before the House of Commons in 1647, and Cromwell's secretary Thurloe consulted him on appointments. In 1654 he became master of Christ's College. His great work, The True Intellectual System of the Universe, appeared in 1678. Its first part set out to confute all the reason and philosophy of atheism. No more of it was published, perhaps because of the outcry the first part raised. He died on 26 June 1688.
britannica-1911-dahlmann-friedrich-chris:
Friedrich Christoph Dahlmann, a German historian and politician, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in May seventeen eighty five, he came from an old Hanseatic family of Wismar. His father, the mayor of the town, meant him to study theology. His own bent was toward the study of classical tongues.

He studied at Copenhagen and Halle in the early eighteen hundreds. After his studies he translated some Greek tragic poets and a comedy of Aristophanes. He was also drawn to modern literature and philosophy. The troubles of the times touched him in person, and the entry follows how they shaped his path.
britannica-1911-enneking-john-joseph:
John Joseph Enneking, an American landscape painter born in 1841, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born of German ancestry at Minster, Ohio, and educated at a college in Cincinnati. He served in the American Civil War in 1861 and 1862, then studied art in New York and Boston.

The entry tells of a break in that path. Weak eyes made him give up art, and he turned to making tinware, where he failed. Only then did he return to painting. From 1873 to 1876 he studied in Munich and in Paris, and he later sketched in Holland. The article calls him a painter of open air scenes. His favoured subject was the twilight of a New England November, and the half lights of spring, autumn, and winter.
britannica-1911-epitaph:
An epitaph, strictly, is a text cut upon a tomb. The 1911 Britannica entry takes the word from Greek parts that mean upon and a tomb. By plain growth of use, the name now fits any piece writ as if for a tomb, whether it is cut there or not.

The entry notes the word came into English in an old form used by early poets. Many of the best known such pieces, old and new, are mere book tributes that never sat on stone. The intent of the writer may have failed, or may never have been to cut the words at all. The piece still counts if it fits the use. One hard rule rules the form: a text meant for a wall must be short.
britannica-1911-erskine-ralph:
Ralph Erskine, a Scottish divine who lived from 1685 to 1752, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the brother of Ebenezer Erskine and was born in March 1685. He studied at the university of Edinburgh and was ordained as assistant minister at Dunfermline. He backed the protests his brother laid on the table of the assembly.

He did not in form leave the set church till 1737, though he sat at the first meeting of the associate presbytery. When that body split over an oath laid on burgesses, he and his brother held with the burgher side. He died after a short illness in November 1752. His works are sermons, verse paraphrases, and gospel sonnets. The Gospel Sonnets have been printed on their own many times. His life and diary were put out in 1842.
britannica-1911-eucken-rudolf-christoph:
Rudolf Christoph Eucken (1846– ), German philosopher, was born on 5 January 1846 at Aurich in East Friesland. His father died in his childhood, and his mother raised him. At Aurich the philosopher Wilhelm Reuter taught him and shaped his thought. At Göttingen he took his degree in classical philology and ancient history. In Berlin he studied under Trendelenburg, whose ethical cast drew him strongly. He taught at Basel from 1871 to 1874, then took the Jena chair.

In 1908 he received the Nobel prize for literature. His work joins history to construction. The historical books tie each age's concepts to the age itself. The constructive side he called Activism: a vital religious drive applied to society's practical problems. All philosophy, for Eucken, is philosophy of life, not bare intellect. His chief books include a history of modern concepts, studies of great thinkers' views of life, and works on religion and history.
britannica-1911-falguiere-jean-alexandre:
Jean Alexandre Joseph Falguiere is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Falguiere was a French sculptor and painter, born at Toulouse in 1831. He studied at the Ecole des Beaux Arts in Paris. In 1859 he won the Prix de Rome, the great prize for young artists.

His first notable bronze was the Victor of the Cock-Fight, shown in 1864. Tarcisus the Christian Boy-Martyr followed in 1867, and both works rest in the Luxembourg Museum. A medal of honour at the Salon came in 1868. He was made an officer of the Legion of Honour ten years later. His chief monuments are named: one to Admiral Courbet at Abbeville and a famed Joan of Arc. His Triumph of the Republic, a vast chariot group for the Arc de Triomphe, crowns the list. The entry honours a sculptor France trusted with its heroes.
britannica-1911-fayrer-sir-joseph:
Sir Joseph Fayrer (1824-1907), English physician, was born at Plymouth on 6 December 1824. After study at Charing Cross hospital he became medical officer of H.M.S. Victory in 1847 and saw fighting at Palermo and Rome while travelling with Lord Mount-Edgcumbe. Appointed assistant surgeon in Bengal in 1850, he served in the Burmese campaign of 1852 and was Residency surgeon at Lucknow during the Mutiny.

From 1859 to 1872 Fayrer was professor of surgery at the Medical College of Calcutta, and he accompanied the prince of Wales on his Indian tour as physician. Back in England he presided over the Medical Board of the India Office from 1874 to 1895 and was made a baronet in 1896. He wrote widely on medicine in India, above all on its poisonous snakes in Thanatophidia of India (1872). His Recollections appeared in 1900. He died at Falmouth on 21 May 1907.
britannica-1911-fetis-francois-joseph:
Francois Joseph Fetis (1784-1871), Belgian composer and writer on music, was born at Mons on 25 March 1784 and trained by his father, a musician. His gift showed early: he composed at seven and was organist at Sainte-Waudru at nine. In 1800 he went to Paris and finished his studies at the conservatoire under Boieldieu, Rey and Pradher. In 1806 he set out to revise the Roman liturgical chants back to their original form.

That same year Fetis began his Biographie universelle des musiciens, his most important work, though it did not appear until 1834. He became a professor at the Paris conservatoire in 1821 and founded the Revue musicale in 1827, the first serious French paper devoted only to music. Called by Leopold I in 1833, he directed the Brussels conservatoire and the king's chapel. The entry judges his many compositions, from opera to song, doomed to oblivion, while his writings endure.
britannica-1911-fourier-jean-baptiste-jo:
Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier (1768-1830), French mathematician, was born at Auxerre on 21 March 1768. He was a tailor's son and was left an orphan at eight. A friend's kindness got him into the military school of his native town, then run by Benedictines. He shone as a student, above all in mathematics. Low birth and poverty barred him from the army, so the school made him its professor of mathematics, teaching where he had learned.

In 1787 Fourier became a novice at the abbey of St Benoit-sur-Loire, but he left in 1789 and returned to his college. There he lectured on rhetoric, philosophy and history beside his mathematics. The entry follows him through the Revolution to Egypt and to the prefecture of Grenoble. It ends with the work on heat that made his name, and the series of sines and cosines that still bear it in every textbook of analysis.
britannica-1911-gall-franz-joseph:
Gall, Franz Joseph (1758–1828), the founder of phrenology, was born at Tiefenbrunn near Pforzheim in Baden on the 9th of March 1758. He studied medicine at Strassburg and Vienna and began practice at Vienna in 1785. He built his doctrine that talents depend on the brain and can be read from the shape of the skull. He began lecturing on cranioscopy at Vienna in 1796, until the government banned the lectures in 1802 as dangerous to religion, a ban that only spread his fame.

In 1805 Gall left Vienna with Spurzheim and lectured through Germany, then settled in Paris in 1807. His Anatomie et physiologie du système nerveux, begun in 1810 with Spurzheim's name beside his, was finished in 1819. A charge of atheism he answered in 1811, and in 1819 he became a naturalized Frenchman. A London lecture visit in 1823 fell flat. Disabled by a stroke early in 1828, he died at Montrouge on the 22nd of August that year.
britannica-1911-galloway-joseph:
Joseph Galloway (1731-1803) was an American lawyer and politician, among the most prominent of the Loyalists. The 1911 Britannica entry tracks him from his birth in Anne Arundel county, Maryland, to his rise in Philadelphia law. From 1756 to 1774 he sat in the Pennsylvania Assembly, presiding over it from 1766 to 1773, and with Benjamin Franklin led opposition to the Proprietary government.

As revolution neared, Galloway chose compromise. In the First Continental Congress in 1774 he proposed a plan of union with a crown-appointed president-general and an elected grand council; it failed by six colonies to five. He later joined the British, ran police and port affairs in occupied Philadelphia, and fled to England in 1778, losing property worth 40,000 pounds. The entry also lists his pamphlets and praises his clear political writing.
britannica-1911-garat-dominique-joseph:
Dominique Joseph Garat is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Garat was a French writer and statesman who lived from 1749 to 1833. He was born at Bayonne and had a good schooling. He worked as a lawyer at Bordeaux, then came to Paris. There he met leading writers and wrote for famed journals.

The article tells how praise essays won him prizes from the Academy. In 1785 he became a teacher of history, and his talks drew large crowds. He won a seat in the states general in 1789. Under Danton he became minister of justice in 1792. In that post he had to tell King Louis the Sixteenth his death sentence. He then served as minister of the interior, but proved weak in that role. He resigned in 1793.
britannica-1911-gillott-joseph:
Joseph Gillott, an English maker of steel pens, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Sheffield in seventeen ninety nine, he worked there as a cutler for some time. In eighteen twenty one he moved to Birmingham. There he found work in the steel toy trade, making buckles and chains.

The entry tells how he turned to making steel pens by machine about eighteen thirty. He patented a way to place long points on pen nibs. Later ideas cut the hardness and stiffness that had plagued early nibs. Side slits and cross ground points made the pens flex more. By eighteen fifty nine he had built a very large trade.
britannica-1911-glanvill-joseph:
Joseph Glanvill (1636-1680) was an English philosopher, born at Plymouth in 1636 and educated at Exeter and Lincoln colleges, Oxford. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his church posts after the Restoration. He held livings in Essex and Somerset, then the abbey church at Bath in 1666. A Worcester prebend followed in 1678, and he served as chaplain to Charles II from 1672. He died at Bath in November 1680.

His first work, The Vanity of Dogmatizing of 1661, is the entry's centre. A passage in it suggested Matthew Arnold's Scholar Gipsy. Following Pascal, Glanvill used philosophical doubt as a bulwark for faith. He argued that men know isolated facts but cannot perceive the causal links between them, in words the entry notes Hume would echo. The piece closes with his place in the new philosophy of the Restoration age.
britannica-1911-gobel-jean-baptiste-jose:
Jean Baptiste Joseph Gobel lived from 1727 to 1794 and was a French churchman. The 1911 Britannica life adds that he played a part in politics too. He was born at Thann in Alsace in September 1727. He studied theology at the German College at Rome in youth. Posts in church chapters and as a suffragan bishop followed in turn.

His public life began with the states general in the year 1789. Clergy of the Huningue district sent him there as their deputy. The turn of his life was his oath to the civil constitution. He took that oath on the third of January in 1791. He had backed that new church frame since May of 1790.
britannica-1911-gottsched-johann-christo:
Johann Christoph Gottsched (1700–1766) was a German author and critic. He was born on 2 February 1700 at Judithenkirch near Königsberg, the son of a Lutheran churchman. He studied thought and history at the university of his home town. On taking his degree in 1723, he fled to Leipzig to dodge forced service in the Prussian army. There he had the shield of J. B. Mencke, a known poet and head of a Leipzig society of poets.

Gottsched was chosen as the senior of that society in 1726. The next year he set it up anew as the Deutsche Gesellschaft. In 1730 he was made a professor of poetry at Leipzig, and in 1734 a professor of logic and metaphysics. He died at Leipzig on 12 December 1766. His chief work was his Versuch einer kritischen Dichtkunst of 1730.
britannica-1911-hasse-johann-adolph:
Johann Adolph Hasse (1699-1783) was a German composer born near Hamburg. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his start as a tenor singer in opera. Work at Brunswick brought his first opera, Antigonus, in 1723. The duke then sent him to Italy to finish his training there.

Study at Naples and a hit serenade made his name across Italy. Sesostrato at Naples in 1726 spread that fame still wider. He wed singer Faustina Bordogni in 1730 and moved to Dresden. In London he wisely refused to set himself up against Handel. Long Dresden service followed, with late operas still written in Vienna.
britannica-1911-howe-joseph:
Joseph Howe (1804–1873) was a Canadian statesman, born at Halifax, Nova Scotia, on the 13th of December 1804. His father, John Howe, was a United Empire Loyalist, long king's printer and postmaster-general for the Maritime Provinces. Joseph had little regular schooling and entered his father's office at thirteen. In 1827 he started the Acadian, a weekly journal, and in 1828 bought the Nova Scotian.

In 1835 Howe was prosecuted for libelling the Halifax magistrates. No lawyer would take his case, so he pleaded it himself, and won acquittal with a speech of over six hours. That speech won freedom of the press for Nova Scotia and made his name as an orator. In 1836 he entered the assembly. The long life follows his fight for responsible government, his part in Confederation's quarrels, and his later years in the government of the new dominion.
britannica-1911-hume-joseph:
Joseph Hume, who lived from 1777 to 1855, was a British politician born at Montrose in Scotland. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from medical study at Edinburgh to a surgeon post in India in 1797. Skill in native tongues and in business won him rich offices there fast. Interpreter and commissary general posts lined his purse in those early years.

In 1802 his chemistry saved a vast store of damp spoiled gunpowder for the army. Peace in 1808 let him resign and sail home with forty thousand pounds in hand. Travel and a verse version of Dante Inferno filled the years to 1812. That year he bought a seat in parliament and began his long career.
britannica-1911-jacotot-joseph:
Joseph Jacotot (1770-1840) was a French teacher known for a method he called intellectual emancipation, and his life fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dijon, he taught Latin there at age nineteen, then studied law and worked as a lawyer. He also gave much time to maths.

The entry follows his part in the French Revolution, his army service in Belgium in 1792, and his posts at the Polytechnic school. It notes his early teaching tests at Dijon and his later chairs in maths and Roman law. After the empire fell, he left France, settled in Brussels, and taught French at the university there from 1818.
britannica-1911-joachim-joseph:
Joseph Joachim was a German fife star and tune smith who lived from eighteen thirty-one to nineteen seven. He was born near Pressburg, the son of Jewish folk. His folk moved to Budapest when he was two. He played in a hall show at age eight.

Study in Vienna and Leipzig honed his art, and a famed tune lord took him up. A London show in his teens caused a stir. Posts at Weimar and Hanover brought him close to the great names of his age. He brought a young peer to the heed of Schumann, a famed tale of that time.
britannica-1911-joubert-joseph:
Joseph Joubert (1754-1824) was a French moralist born at Montignac on 6 May 1754. He made his studies at Toulouse and spent some years there as a teacher. Weak health proved too much for that work. After two years of study at home he went to Paris early in 1778. There he joined the heads of the philosophic party, above all Diderot, whose pupil he in a sense was.

Joubert's closest bond was with the abbe de Fontanes. In 1790 his home town called him back to serve as a justice of the peace. He did that work with great care. His gift flowered in the calm home of Mme de Beaumont, whom he had met in flight from the Terror. Her death in 1803 was a hard blow. His writing, never large in bulk, fell off from that time.
britannica-1911-keane-john-joseph:
John Joseph Keane (1839– ) was an American Roman Catholic archbishop. He was born in Ballyshannon, Ireland, on the 12th of September 1839, and his family settled in America when he was seven. He was trained at Saint Charles's College in Maryland and at Saint Mary's Seminary, Baltimore, and in 1866 he was ordained priest and made curate of St Patrick's in Washington.

On the 25th of August 1878 he was consecrated Bishop of Richmond, following James Gibbons. There he set up the Confraternity of the Holy Ghost and founded schools and churches for black Catholics. In 1886 he became rector of the Catholic University at Washington, and he did much to build it up. His democratic and liberal course made him enemies at Rome. In 1896 a request came from Rome for his resignation of the rectorate, and he spent 1897 to 1900 in Rome itself.
britannica-1911-kenngott-gustav-adolph: Gustav Adolph Kenngott (1818–1897) was a German mineralogist, born at Breslau on the 6th of January 1818. After work in the court mineral cabinet at Vienna, he became professor of mineralogy at the university of Zürich. He stood out for his research in mineralogy, crystallography, and petrology, and he died at Lugano on the 7th of March 1897. His books include textbooks of crystallography and of mineralogy. The second reached a fifth edition in 1880. He also wrote a survey of mineral research and a work on the minerals of Switzerland.
britannica-1911-lagrange-chancel-francoi:
François Joseph de Lagrange-Chancel (1677–1758), French dramatist and satirist, was born at Périgueux on the 1st of January 1677. Precocious, he produced a play at Bordeaux at nine, and at fourteen his mother took him to Paris, where the princesse de Conti became his patron. His tragedy Jugurtha, later called Adherbal, was performed in 1694 with Racine's advice. Oreste et Pylade, Méléagre, Amasis and Ino et Mélicerte followed, and he rose at court to be maître d'hôtel to the duchess of Orleans.

His prosperity ended in 1720 with his Philippiques, odes accusing the regent, Philip of Orleans, of the most odious crimes. He found sanctuary at Avignon but was lured beyond the papal boundary, arrested, and imprisoned on the isles of Sainte Marguerite. He escaped to Sardinia and passed on to Spain and Holland, where his fourth and fifth Philippiques appeared.
britannica-1911-lakanal-joseph:
Joseph Lakanal (1762–1845), French politician, was born at Serres in Ariège on the 14th of July 1762. His name, originally Lacanal, was altered to set him apart from his Royalist brothers. He taught for fourteen years in the schools of a teaching congregation. When his department elected him to the Convention in 1792 he was vicar to his uncle, bishop of Pamiers. In the Convention he kept apart from the party sections, though he voted for the death of Louis XVI.

His great service was in education. He joined the Committee of Public Instruction early in 1793 and carried decrees on monuments, schools and the Museum of Natural History. On the 26th of June he brought forward his Projet d'éducation nationale. It proposed primary schooling paid from public funds, secondary education left to private enterprise, and a central commission. The Convention refused the scheme and referred the question to a commission.
britannica-1911-lancaster-joseph:
Joseph Lancaster, an English educationist who lived from 1778 to 1838, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Southwark, the son of a Chelsea pensioner, he had few chances for steady schooling. At age twenty he began to teach a few poor children in his fathers house. He charged no fee save a trifle where parents could pay.

Soon a thousand children filled rooms in Borough Road, and rich patrons gave funds for a schoolroom. His plan rested on older pupils who served as monitors. Set drills let those young teachers pass on reading, writing, and sums to large groups at once. Tools were scant, with torn spelling leaves pasted on boards and sand spread on a desk. The order and cheer of the school drew wide notice. That notice came at a time when the schooling of the poor was near wholly neglected.
britannica-1911-le-bon-joseph:
Joseph Le Bon, a French politician who lived from 1765 to 1795, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Arras, he became a priest and taught rhetoric at Beaune. He took up the ideas of the Revolution and joined the Constitutional Church. He later served as mayor of Arras and sat in the Convention from July 1793.

Le Bon was sent on missions to the Somme and Pas de Calais areas. There he dealt with foes of the Revolution with great harshness. After the turn against the men of terror, he was arrested and tried. He was put to death at Amiens in October 1795 for abuse of power. The entry adds a fair note in his favour. His courage had saved Cambrai from falling to the Austrians.
britannica-1911-le-conte-joseph:
Joseph Le Conte, who lived from 1823 to 1901, was an American geologist of Huguenot stock. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born in Liberty county, Georgia, on the twenty-sixth of February 1823. He took a degree at Franklin College, then read medicine in New York. After a few years of practice he went to Harvard. There he learned natural history under Agassiz, and a field trip fired his love of geology.

Le Conte taught in Georgia and then in South Carolina, in chairs of science and geology. In 1869 he took the chair of geology at the university of California, which he held till his death. His books include a standard Elements of Geology and works on faith, science, and evolution. He led both the chief American science body and its geology society. He died in the Yosemite Valley in 1901.
britannica-1911-lefebvre-pierre-francois:
Pierre François Joseph Lefebvre, duke of Danzig and marshal of France, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He lived from 1755 to 1820 and was born at Rouffach in Alsace in October 1755. At the outbreak of the Revolution he was a sergeant in the Gardes françaises. With many of his comrades he took the popular side. He stood out for bravery and humanity in the street fights of Paris.

Lefebvre rose to general of division in 1794. At Stockach in 1799 he was badly wounded and returned to France, where he helped Napoleon in the coup of 18 Brumaire. He was among the first generals made marshal under the Empire. He commanded the guard infantry at Jena and conducted the siege of Danzig, from which he took his title. He led a corps in Spain and the Imperial Guard in Russia.
britannica-1911-leidy-joseph:
Leidy, Joseph is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American naturalist and student of fossils. Born in Philadelphia on the ninth of September 1823, Leidy taught himself mineralogy and botany and took a medical degree at the university of Pennsylvania in 1844. In 1853 he became professor of anatomy at Pennsylvania, with a special bent toward comparative anatomy, and in 1884 he helped found its department of biology and led it.

His papers on biology and fossil life were very many, running from microscopic creatures to the great backboned beasts. His larger works treat the Cretaceous reptiles of the United States and the extinct vertebrate fauna of the western territories. His best known book, though, was a plainer one: an Elementary Treatise on Human Anatomy of 1860, kept alive in new editions.
britannica-1911-leverrier-urbain-jean-jo:
Urbain Jean Joseph Leverrier, who lived from 1811 to 1877, was a French astronomer born at Saint Lo. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how his father strove to send him to Paris for study. A fine exam won him entry to the Ecole Polytechnique in 1831. Top honours there let him choose his branch of public service freely.

He picked the tobacco office and did chemical work under Gay Lussac at first. Two papers on phosphorus compounds showed his ability in print by 1837. That year the astronomy teaching post at his school fell vacant by chance. He took it, and a new calling in the stars began for him.
britannica-1911-magnetograph:
Magnetograph names a tool that keeps a non-stop record of changes in the earth's magnetism, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains how it works. It tracks three things: the direction of the needle, and the sideways and downward pull of the field. The tool shows only how these values shift over time. Their true size is fixed by separate checks made nearby with other instruments.

For direction, a magnet hangs from a long fibre and carries a small mirror. Light falls through a slit onto that mirror and onto a fixed one, and the two spots are thrown onto photographic paper wrapped round a drum turned by clockwork. The fixed mirror draws a straight base line. The moving spot wanders to one side or the other as the field changes, and the gap between the lines shows how far and when.
britannica-1911-milner-joseph:
Joseph Milner is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English churchman and school head born in seventeen forty four. He was schooled at Leeds and at Cambridge and then worked as a curate. He later ran a grammar school in Hull and preached in its main church.

The entry notes his strong push for the church revival of his day in Hull. He also cared for a small parish a few miles from the town. His essays and sermons were printed, but one large work made his name. That work told the full history of the church. His brother finished the last parts and reissued the whole set after his death.
britannica-1911-monotriglyph: Monotriglyph, in architecture, is the spacing of the Doric column in which only one triglyph comes between the triglyphs over the axes of the columns. A brief 1911 Britannica article defines it so, and calls that the usual arrangement. It gives one famed exception, in the Propylaea at Athens. There two triglyphs stand over the central spacing, to give more width to the roadway. Up that road chariots and beasts for sacrifice ascended.
britannica-1911-montagu-ralph:
Ralph Montagu, 1st Duke of Montagu (c. 1638–1709), was an English diplomat. He was the second son of Edward, 2nd Baron Montagu of Boughton. That peerage was one of a set given in the 17th century to men of the Montagu family. The line runs back to Sir Edward Montagu, chief justice in the time of Henry VIII. He was grandfather of the first earl of Manchester and of Edward, 1st Baron Montagu of Boughton.

That first baron was put in the Tower by parliament for his loyalty to Charles I. His son Edward, the 2nd baron, took the side of parliament in the Civil War. He was one of the lords who led the king from Newark to Holmby House in 1647. He had two sons, of whom Ralph was the younger. The elder, Edward, was master of the horse to Queen Catherine.
britannica-1911-moore-albert-joseph:
Albert Joseph Moore was an English painter of fair scenes who lived from eighteen forty-one to eighteen ninety-three. He was born at York, the last of fourteen young of a painter of the north. Two of his kin also rose to fame with the brush. His love of art showed young, and kin urged him on.

He sent work to the chief show at age sixteen and soon chose to work on his own. Wall work for great homes and church walls filled his first years. A first big work came from a stay in Rome. His next works fixed the pure craft view that ruled all his later art.
britannica-1911-mortier-edouard-adolphe-:
Edouard Adolphe Casimir Joseph Mortier, duke of Treviso and marshal of France, was born at Cateau Cambrésis on 13 February 1768 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered the army as a sub lieutenant in 1791. Campaigns on the north eastern frontier and in the Netherlands filled 1792 and 1793 for him. Service on the Meuse and the Rhine came after.

In the war of 1799 he rose in step from general of brigade to general of division. His conduct in the occupation of Hanover drew the eye of Napoleon. That notice put him on the first list of marshals created in 1804. He led a corps in the Ulm campaign and shone at Dürrenstein in bright style. Hanover and Friedland gave him fresh fields in 1806 and 1807. A dukedom of Treviso was his reward in 1808.
britannica-1911-naquet-alfred-joseph:
Alfred Joseph Naquet, a French chemist and politician born in 1834, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Carpentras, he became a professor in the medical faculty at Paris in 1863. That same year he also taught chemistry at Palermo, giving his lectures in Italian. In 1867 he lost his post and his civic rights.

The loss came with a prison term of fifteen months for his part in a secret society. A new case over a book on religion, property, and family drove him to refuge in Spain in 1869. Back in France, he took an active part in the revolution of September 1870. In the National Assembly he sat on the extreme left. His name is linked above all with the campaign to restore divorce in French law.
britannica-1911-pandulph:
Pandulph, a Roman church politician and papal legate to England who died in 1226, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Rome, he first came to England in 1211 on a mission. He was commissioned by Pope Innocent the Third to negotiate with King John. He obtained no satisfactory concessions from the king on that visit.

 In May 1213 he came again to receive the submission of the king at Dover. On the next day John surrendered England to Rome of his own motion, to receive it again as a papal fief. Pandulph repaid that act by using every means to avert a French invasion of England. He was present at Runnymede in 1215, when the great charter was signed, and John rewarded him with the see of Norwich.
britannica-1911-pantograph:
Pantograph is a tool for copying a flat drawing at a smaller, larger, or equal size. The 1911 Britannica article takes its name from Greek words for all and for writing. In its common form the tool has two long arms joined at one end, and two short arms joined to them. The four arms form a shape that stays a parallelogram at any angle. The tool rests on small wheels and moves freely over the paper.

Tubes on the arms hold a fixed pivot, a tracing point, and a pencil, and the three can be swapped. When the three points stand in one straight line, the pencil tracks the tracer in a fixed ratio. So it draws a copy cut down by that ratio. Swapping pencil and tracer gives a blown-up copy. Marks on the arms show where to set the sliders for the ratios in common use.
britannica-1911-papineau-louis-joseph:
Louis Joseph Papineau was a Canadian rebel leader and politician of Lower Canada. He lived from seventeen eighty six to eighteen seventy one. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Montreal, the son of a notary and assembly member, he studied law.

Papineau was schooled at the seminary of Quebec, where oratory gifts grew. He joined the bar in eighteen ten and the assembly in eighteen o eight. By eighteen fifteen he was speaker and head of the French Canadian party. Many wrongs in the land cried out for redress in that era. In eighteen twenty three he went to England to fight a union plan. His stand against the government grew firmer with each passing year.
britannica-1911-parker-joseph:
Joseph Parker (1830–1902) was an English Nonconformist churchman, born at Hexham-on-Tyne on 9 April 1830. His father was a stonemason. Parker picked up a fair schooling and kept adding to it all his life. From 1845 to 1850, as a local preacher and a voice for temperance, he won a name for strong speech. He was shaped by Thomas Cooper, the Chartist, and by Edward Miall. He was also close to Joseph Cowen, later a member of parliament for Newcastle.

In 1852 Parker wrote to Dr John Campbell of London for advice on the ministry. After a short trial he became Campbell's helper, and he went to talks on logic and thought at University College. From 1853 to 1858 he was pastor at Banbury. His next post was at Cavendish Street in Manchester.
britannica-1911-pennell-joseph:
Joseph Pennell, an American artist and author born in 1860, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Philadelphia on the fourth of July 1860 and first studied there. Like his friend Whistler, he then went to Europe and made his home in London. He wrote many books, a good share of them with his wife, Elizabeth Robins Pennell.

His chief fame is as an etcher and lithographer of new bent, and as an illustrator. Their close bond with Whistler led the Pennells to take up a life of that artist in 1906. A court fight with his executrix over the right to use his letters held the book back. It came out in 1908. The article is a note on a man still at work, and it keeps to the bones of his career and his craft.
britannica-1911-perthes-friedrich-christ:
Friedrich Christoph Perthes (1772–1843) was a German publisher, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his start in the book trade. He was born at Rudolstadt on the twenty first of April 1772. At fifteen he became an apprentice to a bookseller in Leipzig. He stayed with that master for about six years.

Perthes settled in Hamburg in 1793 as an aide to another bookseller. In 1796 he set up a bookselling business of his own there. Two years later he took his brother in law into partnership. That partner was Johann Heinrich Besser, who lived from 1775 to 1826. In 1797 Perthes married a daughter of the poet Matthias Claudius. The marriage brought him close to a circle of Protestant writers. That circle had a strong effect on the growth of his religious views.
britannica-1911-phillimore-sir-robert-jo:
Sir Robert Joseph Phillimore, an English judge born at Whitehall in eighteen ten, was the son of a known church lawyer. He was schooled at Westminster and at Christ Church, Oxford. There a lifelong friendship with Gladstone began for him. His first post was a clerkship in the board of control. He left it in eighteen thirty five and turned to law.
